title: How Indexing Works in SQL
intro: A practical guide to designing, reading and troubleshooting SQL Server indexes for real application workloads.

sections.title: 1. What an index does
sections.body: At the logical level, a table looks like rows and columns. Physically, SQL Server stores table data in 8 KB data pages. The number of rows in a page depends on row size, so a page may contain many narrow rows or only a few wide rows. An index adds an organized path that helps SQL Server find the right pages without reading the whole table.
sections.note: Indexes improve reads by adding a maintained access path, but they consume storage and must be updated when the table changes.
sections.scenario: A customer order page that searches by CustomerId can avoid scanning millions of orders after an appropriate index is created.

sections.title: 2. Clustered indexes
sections.body: A clustered index defines the logical order of the table data and forms a B-tree structure. The root and intermediate pages contain index keys and pointers; the leaf pages contain the actual table rows. A table can have only one clustered index because it can have only one clustered row order. A primary key is commonly clustered, but that is a design choice rather than a rule.
sections.example:
CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX CX_Orders_OrderId
ON dbo.Orders (OrderId);
sections.note: Choose a narrow, stable and commonly used key. Randomly changing wide keys can cause page splits and extra storage overhead.
sections.scenario: An Orders table may use an increasing OrderId as its clustered key so new orders are appended efficiently.

sections.title: 3. Non-clustered indexes
sections.body: A non-clustered index is a separate B-tree containing indexed key values and row locators. Its root and intermediate pages guide the search, while its leaf pages contain the key and a pointer to the clustered row or heap row. When the query asks for columns not stored in the non-clustered index, SQL Server may use that locator and the clustered index to fetch the remaining columns. A table can have multiple non-clustered indexes, each supporting a different access pattern.
sections.example:
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Status_CreatedAt
ON dbo.Orders (Status, CreatedAt);
sections.note: The key order matters. This index is most useful when queries filter by Status and then search or sort by CreatedAt.
sections.scenario: A support queue that loads pending orders newest first can benefit from a composite non-clustered index.

sections.title: 4. Composite index key order
sections.body: A composite index contains multiple key columns. Put columns used in equality predicates first, followed by range, sorting or grouping columns when that matches the dominant query pattern.
sections.example:
CREATE INDEX IX_Tickets_Tenant_Status_CreatedAt
ON dbo.Tickets (TenantId, Status, CreatedAt DESC);

SELECT TicketId, CreatedAt, Priority
FROM dbo.Tickets
WHERE TenantId = @TenantId
  AND Status = 'Open'
ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC;
sections.note: The same columns in a different order may support a different query. Do not assume one composite index serves every combination of filters.
sections.scenario: A multi-tenant support system can seek directly to open tickets for one tenant instead of scanning other tenants' data.

sections.title: 5. Included columns and covering indexes
sections.body: An included column is stored at the leaf level without becoming part of the index key. An index that contains all columns needed by a query is called a covering index and may avoid lookups to the base table.
sections.note: Include only useful output columns. Very wide indexes increase storage, memory pressure and write cost.
sections.scenario: An order summary endpoint can return common display fields directly from the index instead of performing a lookup for every matching order.

sections.title: 6. Filtered indexes
sections.body: A filtered index covers only rows that meet a predicate. It is useful when an application repeatedly queries a small, stable subset of a much larger table.
sections.example:
CREATE INDEX IX_Orders_Pending
ON dbo.Orders (CreatedAt)
INCLUDE (CustomerId, TotalAmount)
WHERE Status = 'Pending';
sections.note: The query predicate must be compatible with the filter, and the filtered condition should match a real workload rather than a temporary data distribution.
sections.scenario: A payment worker that repeatedly finds pending orders can use a smaller filtered index instead of indexing every completed historical order.

sections.title: 7. How SQL Server finds a row
sections.body: For a selective predicate such as EmployeeId = 1120, SQL Server starts at the root page, follows the pointer for the key range 801-1200, moves to the leaf page containing rows 1001-1200, and then finds row 1120. This is an index seek: the B-tree avoids reading unrelated pages. The execution plan can show Number of Rows Read = 1 and Actual Number of Rows = 1. Without a useful index, SQL Server may scan every data page instead.
sections.note: Use the actual execution plan and logical reads to decide whether an operator is expensive for the data volume and request frequency.
sections.scenario: A query that was fast with 10,000 rows may need an index after the same table grows to 100 million rows.

sections.title: 8. Seek, scan and key lookup in the execution plan
sections.body: An index seek navigates directly to matching keys. An index scan reads many or all index pages, which can be reasonable for a large result but is often expensive for a one-row lookup. A non-clustered seek may be followed by a key lookup when the index finds the key but does not contain every selected column.
sections.example:
-- Clustered seek: Id is indexed
SELECT *
FROM dbo.Employees
WHERE Id = 932000;

-- Scan: Name has no useful index
SELECT *
FROM dbo.Employees
WHERE Name = 'ABC 932000';

-- Non-clustered seek may fetch missing columns
CREATE INDEX IX_Employees_Name
ON dbo.Employees (Name);
sections.sample:
Employees: 1,000,000 rows
Target Id = 932000
Target Name = ABC 932000
sections.output:
Clustered seek: rows read 1, rows returned 1
Name scan: rows read 1,000,000, rows returned 1
Non-clustered seek + key lookup: key found, clustered row fetched
sections.note: Read execution plans from the result operation back toward the scan or seek. Compare rows read with rows returned, and use an INCLUDE column or a covering index only when the measured lookup cost justifies the extra write and storage cost.
sections.scenario: A production API can look healthy in row count but still be slow if a non-clustered index causes thousands of key lookups for a wide result set.

sections.title: 9. SARGable predicates
sections.body: A SARGable predicate lets SQL Server use an index efficiently. Applying a function or calculation to the indexed column often prevents a direct seek. Rewrite the predicate when possible.
sections.note: Avoid wrapping indexed columns in functions, implicit conversions or expressions unless you have measured the plan and understand the tradeoff.
sections.scenario: A yearly report can use the CreatedAt index with a date range instead of calculating YEAR for every row.

sections.title: 10. Selectivity and cardinality
sections.body: Selectivity describes how narrowly a predicate identifies rows. A unique CustomerId is usually more selective than a Yes/No IsActive flag. SQL Server estimates row counts using statistics, and inaccurate estimates can lead to poor plans.
sections.note: An index on a low-cardinality column may still help when combined with other keys or when the filtered subset is small.
sections.scenario: An IsActive index may not help a table where 99% of users are active, while a unique email lookup is highly selective.

sections.title: 11. Statistics and execution plans
sections.body: Statistics help the optimizer estimate how many rows a predicate will return. The actual execution plan shows what SQL Server really did, including seeks, scans, joins, lookups, sorts and warnings.
sections.note: Refresh statistics carefully and measure before and after. FULLSCAN can be expensive on large production tables.
sections.scenario: After a bulk import, stale statistics may cause SQL Server to choose a nested-loop plan that is poor for the new data volume.

sections.title: 12. Key lookups
sections.body: A key lookup occurs when SQL Server finds rows in a non-clustered index but must visit the clustered index or heap to fetch additional columns. A few lookups may be fine; thousands can be expensive.
sections.note: A covering index can remove the lookup, but do not automatically include every selected column. Compare the read improvement with write and storage cost.
sections.scenario: An API returning 50,000 matching rows may spend more time performing lookups than reading the original filtered index.

sections.title: 13. Fragmentation and page splits
sections.body: Frequent inserts, updates and deletes can leave index pages fragmented. Random keys can cause page splits when SQL Server inserts into full pages. Fragmentation is a symptom to investigate, not a reason to rebuild every index blindly.
sections.example:
SELECT OBJECT_NAME(ips.object_id) AS TableName,
       i.name AS IndexName,
       ips.avg_fragmentation_in_percent,
       ips.page_count
FROM sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(DB_ID(), NULL, NULL, NULL, 'LIMITED') AS ips
JOIN sys.indexes AS i
  ON i.object_id = ips.object_id
 AND i.index_id = ips.index_id
WHERE ips.page_count > 100;
sections.note: Maintenance decisions should consider fragmentation, page count, workload and maintenance windows. Reorganize and rebuild have different costs.
sections.scenario: A nightly maintenance job can target large, heavily fragmented indexes rather than blocking the entire database with unnecessary rebuilds.

sections.title: 14. Index maintenance choices
sections.body: REORGANIZE is generally an online, incremental operation. REBUILD recreates the index and can be more thorough but may consume more resources and require stronger locking depending on edition and options.
sections.note: Test edition support, transaction log growth, blocking and available maintenance windows before using ONLINE or large rebuilds.
sections.scenario: A high-traffic e-commerce database may reorganize moderate fragmentation during the day and reserve rebuilds for a controlled maintenance window.

sections.title: 15. Indexes and write performance
sections.body: Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE may need to maintain affected indexes. Too many overlapping indexes slow writes, increase log volume and consume memory. Index design must balance read speed with write cost.
sections.example:
SELECT OBJECT_NAME(i.object_id) AS TableName,
       i.name AS IndexName,
       ius.user_seeks, ius.user_scans, ius.user_updates
FROM sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats AS ius
JOIN sys.indexes AS i
  ON i.object_id = ius.object_id
 AND i.index_id = ius.index_id
WHERE ius.database_id = DB_ID();
sections.note: Usage statistics reset after restart or database events, so treat them as evidence over an observation period rather than absolute truth.
sections.scenario: A write-heavy order ingestion service may need fewer indexes than a read-heavy reporting database using the same tables.

sections.title: 16. Debugging a slow query
sections.body: Start with the actual query, parameter values, row counts and execution plan. Check logical reads, duration, waits, blocking, implicit conversions and whether the estimated and actual row counts differ significantly.
sections.note: Do not add an index based only on a missing-index suggestion. Validate the workload, existing indexes, write cost and whether a query rewrite is better.
sections.scenario: When an endpoint slows after a release, compare the old and new plans and parameter values before changing production indexes.

sections.title: 17. A practical indexing workflow
sections.body: Index from measured workload patterns: capture the important queries, inspect plans, identify predicates and sort order, test a focused index, measure reads and writes, then monitor it after deployment.
sections.note: An index is successful when it improves a real workload without creating unacceptable write, storage or maintenance costs.
sections.scenario: For an enterprise search screen, test representative tenants and date ranges instead of benchmarking only a small development database.
